##### Nigerian AI Startup Khaime Raises USD 500 K Pre-Seed Funding Led By Launch Africa Ventures
Khaime, a Nigerian startup building an AI-powered commerce platform, has raised USD 500 K in pre-seed funding in a round led by Launch Africa Ventures, with participation from angel investors and early friends-and-family backers.

Founded by Gabriel Olokunwolu, Khaime is building a commerce platform for human shoppers and AI agents that increasingly handle product discovery, price comparisons, purchase negotiations, and transactions on consumers’ behalf.

The startup is betting on a shift towards agentic commerce, where merchants will need digital storefronts capable of interacting directly with AI-powered shopping assistants.

The funding will support Khaime’s development as it builds infrastructure for merchants to transact with both traditional online shoppers and autonomous shopping agents.

How Seed Funding For African Startups Creates Jobs and Wealth
web.description:
Every year, thousands of African founders build something worth funding. **Seed funding for African startups** seems to be a bottle-neck for most founders in Africa.

Outline

In 2025, African startups raised somewhere between $3.8 billion and $4.1 billion in total, depending on which tracker you trust. Debt financing alone hit a record $1.64 billion, up 63% year on year.

Pre-seed funding, the earliest money a founder can access, stalled at just $46.5 million across 281 deals in 2025, barely 1.5% of total venture investment on the continent, according to the African Business Angel Network’s 2025 Angel Investment Report, produced with the UNDP and Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Of the startups that raised seed funding in 2022, only about 10 in 100 had closed a Series A within 34 months, based on Condia’s State of Startup Funding in Africa report.

## Seed Funding For African Startups: The Current State (2025-2026 Data)
Here’s what the data actually shows, without the spin that often comes with fundraising headlines.

Equity financing, the traditional form of venture capital where investors take a stake in the company, grew more modestly, rising 8% year on year to $2.4 billion across 462 deals. Deal count stayed almost flat, up just 1% from the year before.

The picture gets more serious at pre-seed.

There is a bright spot worth noting. AVCA’s mid-year report found that seed-stage funding actually climbed 40% to $171 million across 82 early-stage transactions in the first half of 2025 alone.

The conversion numbers tell the rest of the story. Of the cohort that raised seed funding in 2021, only 5.1% successfully raised a Series A within two years. For the 2022 cohort, that figure was 4.2%. Condia’s independent analysis found a similar pattern: of 105 African startups that raised seed funding in 2022, only 10 had closed a Series A within 34 months.

If you are raising seed money right now, this context should shape how you plan.

## Why African Startups Struggle to Raise Seed Capital
The funding gap at the seed stage isn’t random. It comes from a handful of specific, well-documented causes.

Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, and Egypt captured 72% of total startup funding in 2025, and within those four countries, the top ten investments alone accounted for 51% of total deal value. If you are building outside these four markets, in Rwanda, Cameroon, Tanzania, or Mozambique, you are competing for a much smaller pool of attention, even if your business fundamentals are just as strong.

Several historic pre-seed investors have either withdrawn from the market or repositioned their funds toward later, safer stages.

Several of Africa’s largest startup markets, Nigeria in particular, have experienced significant currency depreciation in recent years.

Much of Africa’s angel investing still happens informally, through personal networks rather than structured funds. ABAN’s report found that 62 angel networks across 37 countries collectively deployed the disclosed $4.4 million figure, but acknowledged the real total is likely higher, given how much early-stage investing happens outside formal channels.

It means founders need to be more deliberate about who they approach, when, and with what kind of proof.

Many funds active in Africa are still building their own track record on the continent, which makes them naturally more cautious at the earliest, riskiest stage of a company’s life. A first-time fund manager evaluating a pre-seed startup is taking on two layers of uncertainty at once: whether the startup will work, and whether their own thesis about the market will hold up. That double uncertainty pushes a lot of capital toward safer, later-stage deals where the business model is already proven, which is part of why the seed and pre-seed stages feel thinner than the total funding figures suggest.

## Where to Find Seed Funding For African Startups
TLcom Capital invests from seed through Series B, manages over $350 million in assets, and focuses on Nigeria, Kenya, Francophone West Africa, and Egypt, with offices in Lagos, Nairobi, and London. Launch Africa Ventures is an early-stage fund investing at seed and pre-Series A that has raised over $36 million since 2020 and invested $31 million across 133 startups in 22 countries, including Kuda and Peach Payments. Microtraction is widely regarded as one of the most respected seed-stage VCs on the continent. Ingressive Capital offers seed funding of up to $500,000 in exchange for around 10% equity in tech-enabled startups, alongside strategic guidance and networking support. Ajim Capital provides financing from pre-seed to seed with typical check sizes up to $250,000.

Founders Factory Africa has helped ventures collectively raise over $300 million and create more than 3,500 jobs.

**Grants**, or non-dilutive funding, don’t require giving up equity. The Tony Elumelu Foundation’s 2026 Entrepreneurship Programme offers $5,000 in non-refundable seed capital, plus business training and mentorship, and since 2015 it has invested over $100 million across more than 20,000 entrepreneurs in all 54 African countries.

## How Much Seed Funding Can African Startups Raise?
The honest answer is: it depends heavily on your sector, your country, and how much traction you already have. But there are useful benchmarks.

Most African seed rounds fall between $500,000 and $2 million, with pre-money valuations typically between $3 million and $8 million. Fintech startups and those based in Nigeria, Kenya, or Egypt tend to raise toward the higher end of that range, since these markets have deeper investor pools and more comparable deals to benchmark against. Startups in less-covered markets, or in sectors that investors understand less well, often raise less, even with similar traction.

[See alsoHow To Improve Market Access Across African Regional Blocs](https://mohacafrica.org/how-to-improve-market-access-across-african-regional-blocs/)

Grants tend to be much smaller and more standardized. The Tony Elumelu Foundation, for example, offers a flat $5,000 non-refundable grant. Accelerators sit in a different tier entirely: Y Combinator offers around $500,000 in exchange for roughly 7% equity, which is a global benchmark, not an Africa-specific one, but it’s increasingly relevant as more African startups get accepted into the program.

One mistake we see often is founders anchoring their ask to a well-known competitor’s raise rather than their own numbers. Asking for a $10 million valuation with minimal traction, because a competitor raised at that level, tends to backfire. If you raise at an inflated valuation and don’t grow into it, your next round becomes much harder to close. It’s more useful to build your valuation case from your own revenue, user growth, and market size, using recent comparable African deals as a reference point, not a target to match.

## The Future of Seed Funding for African Startups
Diaspora investment is growing as a distinct category.

Debt financing will likely keep growing as a share of total capital, now sitting at 41% of all funding raised in 2025.

The seed-to-Series-A bottleneck is the single biggest structural risk to watch. Unless more capital moves specifically into pre-seed and seed, this bottleneck could constrain Series A and B activity in 2027 and 2028.

Angel investing is likely to become even more central to the earliest stages of funding, filling the gap left by the withdrawal of some historic pre-seed players.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Seed Funding For African Startups
### How much seed funding can an African startup raise?
Most African seed rounds fall between $500,000 and $2 million, with pre-money valuations typically between $3 million and $8 million, though this varies by sector and country. Fintech startups and those based in Nigeria, Kenya, or Egypt tend to raise toward the higher end; startups in less-covered markets often raise less.

### Does the Tony Elumelu Foundation give seed funding?
The foundation’s 2026 Entrepreneurship Programme offers $5,000 in non-refundable seed capital plus business training and mentorship.

web.title: Pre-Seed Funding: A Startup's Guide to Early-Stage Fundraising
web.description:
# Pre-seed funding: A startup’s guide to early-stage fundraising
## What is pre-seed funding?
Pre-seed funding is the earliest investment a startup receives. It's the capital founders raise to turn a raw idea into a validated concept or minimum viable product (MVP), and it's almost always raised with convertible instruments like [Simple Agreements for Future Equity (SAFE)](https://carta.com/learn/startups/fundraising/convertible-securities/safes/). [Startup funding](https://carta.com/learn/startups/fundraising/) is divided into rounds, which include seed, Series A, Series B, and so on. Pre-seed funding is any funding that comes before the seed round. Beyond that, there isn’t much consensus in the startup community about the exact definition of pre-seed funding.

While there's no single path, data from Carta's [State of Pre-Seed report](https://carta.com/data/state-of-pre-seed-q2-2026/) confirms that founders at this stage typically raise capital from a mix of friends and family, angel investors, and pre-seed venture capitalists (VC). This initial investment happens before a company has a finished product or any revenue.

With early-stage funding, investors are looking for signals that you have a deep understanding of the problem you're trying to solve. They want to see your passion, your unique expertise, and your resilience in the face of early challenges.

But some companies now raise early priced rounds, which they refer to as pre-seed.

The goal is not to get lost in semantics, but instead provide resources for the type of funding available to early-stage startups, to ultimately help founders find the right investors.

![](https://images.ctfassets.net/y88td1zx1ufe/3n7yznCuZfKbdXx14cEPHZ/2d2bc54a8bec7db41525cdb6f4ee54d1/fundraising-101-cta.png)

Startup Fundraising 101

[Watch now](https://carta.com/learn/startup-fundraising-101/?ir=classroom)

### Pre-seed vs. seed funding
|  |  |  |
|-|-|-|
|  | **Pre-seed round** | **Seed round** |
| **Primary goal** | Validate the problem and solution | Achieve product-market fit and scale |
| **Focus** | Building the initial product and team | Growing the user base and revenue |
| **Typical amount raised** | Typically a few hundred thousand dollars (for example, ~$250,000-$1 million), though some rounds are smaller or larger | $500,000-$5 million |
| **Equity issued** | SAFEs or convertible notes | SAFEs, convertible notes or preferred stock |
| **Use of funds** | To test your idea | To gain early traction and start selling |

## How much should you raise at a pre-seed round?
There's no universal number, but most pre-seed rounds land between $150,000 and $1 million. [Carta data shows](https://carta.com/data/state-of-pre-seed-q2-2026/) the average instrument is $276,000, with 18% of rounds in the $1–$2.5 million range as of Q1 2026. The right amount is the one that buys you enough runway to hit your next set of milestones.

Aim for 12-24 months of runway. That's usually the window you need to build a product, validate demand, and reach the traction that leads to a seed round. Raise too little and you'll be back out fundraising before you have results to show. Raise too much and you may give away more ownership than the stage warrants.

Current data can anchor your target. In Q2 2026, the average pre-seed instrument on Carta was $276,000, a record high and up 27% year over year, according to Carta's [State of Pre-Seed report](https://carta.com/data/state-of-pre-seed-q2-2026/). Few pre-seed deals exceed $2.5 million, at least in the U.S., so a round in the low-to-mid six figures is well within the norm.

Work backward from your plan. List the milestones that make you fundable at seed, such as a shipped MVP, early users, and key hires, then estimate the cost and timeline to reach them. Add a buffer for the fundraising process itself, which can take months. The figure you land on is your target raise, grounded in a plan rather than a round-number guess.

![](https://images.ctfassets.net/y88td1zx1ufe/6xJ0yc90rSyFndvy9DNQQm/e6e1b1bb2a88caaf12fec91300003b81/Data_minute_benchmark_for_web.png)

# Khaime Secures $500K Pre-Seed for AI-Powered Commerce in Africa
Nigerian startup Khaime, led by Gabriel Olokunwolu, raised $500,000 in a pre-seed round to build commerce infrastructure for human and AI-driven shopping, with Launch Africa Ventures leading the investment.

T

[Tolulope Bamiloye](https://au-startups.com/authors/tolulope-bamiloye)Funding Correspondent · 20 Nov 2026

3 min read

![Khaime Secures $500K Pre-Seed for AI-Powered Commerce in Africa](https://au-startups.com/_next/image?url=%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fbranded-card-7929-1600x900.webp&w=1920&q=75)

Khaime Secures $500K Pre-Seed for AI-Powered Commerce in Africa

[Khaime](https://au-startups.com/startups/khaime), a Lagos-based AI [commerce](https://au-startups.com/sectors/commerce) platform, has closed a $500,000 pre-seed funding round to develop infrastructure for what it terms “agent-driven commerce,” where artificial intelligence agents, not just human shoppers, conduct transactions. The investment, announced on November 18, 2026, was led by [Launch Africa Ventures](https://au-startups.com/startups/launch-africa-ventures), with additional participation from angel investors and earlier friends-and-family backers.

This pre-seed round marks a foundational capital injection for Khaime, which aims to bridge a potential gap in the evolving e-commerce landscape. The platform supports over 120 currencies and local payment methods.

[Launch Africa Ventures](https://au-startups.com/investors/launch-africa-ventures), a pan-African venture capital firm founded in 2020 by [Zachariah George](https://au-startups.com/investors/zachariah-george) and Janade Du Plessis, specializes in seed and pre-Series A investments. The firm has invested in over 180 portfolio companies across 25 African countries through two funds. Its investment in Khaime aligns with its strategy to back startups addressing funding gaps in early-stage African ventures.

## Competitive Landscape and Market Context
Khaime's bet on AI-driven commerce positions it in an emerging niche, distinct from broader payments infrastructure plays by companies like [Paymob](https://au-startups.com/startups/paymob), which raised a $35 million pre-Series C, or [Lumepay](https://au-startups.com/startups/lumepay)'s $6 million pre-seed, which focus on payment rails.

## What This Round Buys
The $500,000 pre-seed capital is earmarked for several critical areas. Further, the funds will support the expansion of selling features across Instagram, WhatsApp, and [TikTok](https://au-startups.com/startups/tiktok), improve the reliability of its AI assistant Khai and merchant controls, and broaden payout options and local payment methods in additional countries. The company also intends to hire more engineering and support staff. This funding provides Khaime with the runway to build out its core technology and validate its agent commerce hypothesis, targeting a market shift that remains largely nascent in Africa.

# Nigeria Tops Africa Startup Funding at $635M [2026]
![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp)

[Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/)

Updated Oct 23, 2026 · 17 min read

[Share on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F&text=Nigeria%20Tops%20Africa%20Startup%20Funding%20at%20%24635M%20%5B2026%5D)[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F)[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F)[Share on Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/submit?url=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2Fnigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026%2F&title=Nigeria%20Tops%20Africa%20Startup%20Funding%20at%20%24635M%20%5B2026%5D)[Copy link](https://shattered.io/nigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026/)

![Nigeria Tops Africa Startup Funding at $635M](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/nigeria-tops-africa-startup-funding-635-million-2026-gen-1024x585.webp)

Nigerian startups raised **$635 million** between January and September 2026, according to data from the tracker Africa: The Big Deal, and that total puts Nigeria back at the top of the continent’s startup-funding table. [BusinessDay reported](https://businessday.ng/technology/article/nigeria-reclaims-africas-startup-funding-lead-as-investment-hits-635m/) that the result is Nigeria’s first lead in African startup funding since 2022. Reports published on October 21 put the figure at 2.6 times the $247 million Nigerian startups raised in the same nine months of 2025.

The deal count rose too, though far less sharply. A total of 77 Nigerian ventures raised funding in the period, up from 70 a year earlier. That gap between a 157% jump in dollars and a 10% rise in deals tells most of the story, because a handful of very large rounds carried the headline number.

Capital is flowing to emerging-market founders well beyond Lagos, as a recent [$300K pre-seed for a Saudi event-tech startup](https://shattered.io/inve-saudi-event-tech-300k-pre-seed-outliers-vc-2026/) showed. Still, Nigeria startup funding is now the clearest signal of where African software demand is heading.

## Nigeria Startup Funding Versus 2025: 2.6 Times the Money
Nigerian startups raised $247 million in January through September 2025 and $635 million in the same window of 2026. That is an increase of $388 million, or about 157%. [Nairametrics framed the result](https://nairametrics.com/2026/10/21/nigeria-reclaims-africas-startup-funding-lead-as-investments-rise-to-635-million/) as a rise in investment to $635 million, and several other Nigerian outlets used near-identical language on October 21.

|-|-|-|-|
| Funding raised by Nigerian startups | $247 million | $635 million | 2.6x (about +157%) |

### How much did Nigerian startups raise in the first nine months of 2026?
Nigerian startups raised $635 million between January and September 2026, according to Africa: The Big Deal data cited by Nigerian and African outlets. Reports published on October 21 gave the figure.

### How does that compare with 2025?
The number of ventures raising at least $100,000 rose from 70 to 77.

### How much did all of Africa raise?
African startups collectively raised approximately $2.16 billion between January and September 2026.

30 African Startups That Raised Funding in 2026 (So Far)
web.description:
African startups raised **$1.44 billion in the first half of 2026** — slightly ahead of the $1.42 billion raised in H1 2025, but across far fewer deals: just 146 disclosed rounds versus 252 a year earlier. Here are 30 companies that actually got funded this year, and what each deal tells you about where capital is flowing.

The numbers come from [TechCabal Insights](https://insights.techcabal.com/1-44-billion-raised-in-the-first-half-of-2026/), whose trackers put the half-year split at $749 million in Q1 and $692 million in Q2 — $818 million in equity, $614 million in debt and $9 million in grants. [Africa: The Big Deal](https://www.linkedin.com/company/africa-the-big-deal/), which counts only $100k+ deals, tracked $843 million across 160 deals from January to May, split almost evenly between equity and debt — a marked shift from 12–18 months ago, when equity's share sat above 70 percent.

One caveat before the list: not every raise is announced with a press release, and several strong deals this year were undisclosed. Amounts are as disclosed by the companies or tracked by TechCabal Insights, Africa: The Big Deal and our own database.

## The growth rounds: debt does the heavy lifting
**GoCab** raised a **$45 million** hybrid round in February — equity from E3 Capital and JANNGO Capital plus significant debt — to scale ride-hailing in Francophone West Africa.

**MAX** raised **$32 million** in equity and asset-backed financing, starting with a $24 million January round, to finance vehicles for commercial drivers and push its fleet electric.

$4M–$15M • Series A & big seeds

## The Series A club — and Morocco's quiet breakout
**WafR** raised a **$4 million seed** in January for retail-tech, and **Enakl** took **$2.3 million** to modernise shared commuting in Casablanca.

Under $3M • Seed & pre-seed

## The early-stage survivors: small cheques, sharp theses
Early-stage equity was the hardest money to raise in 2026 — which makes the companies that closed rounds worth studying.

In AI, Nairobi's **AethexAI** raised a **$3 million pre-seed** led by 4DX Ventures and Enza Capital to build customer-support and voice automation for African markets ( [our full breakdown](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/aethexai-raises-3-million-2026)).

**Zimi Charge** raised **$2.6 million** from the Development Bank of Southern Africa and Keyo Ventures for EV charging in South Africa. **Breaze Delivery** raised **R20 million (~$1.23 million)** from Knife Capital and Kalon Venture Partners for township e-commerce logistics ( [our coverage](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/breaze-delivery-raises-2026)), and **Eja-Ice** secured **$1 million** from All On for off-grid solar cold-chain in Nigeria ( [deal notes](https://startupmaphub.com/blog/eja-ice-raises-1-million-2026)).

## What these 30 deals tell you about 2026
Half the money went to seven companies; meanwhile 26 startups raised above $100k in January — the lowest tally since at least 2020. If you're raising a $5–15 million round right now, you're in the most competitive segment of the market.
